hero.title: A jail for your AI coding agent
hero.lede: Your coding agent, the program that edits and runs code for you, runs with your user account, so it can read everything you can: the keys to your servers, your cloud account, every other project on the disk. ai-jail starts it inside a sandbox, a fence the operating system holds around one program, built to stop a trusted agent's mistakes. The project is writable. Your keys, your home directory and your shell secrets (the tokens and passwords a terminal keeps in environment variables) are not there.
hero.logoAlt: A padlock made of circuit traces. Behind the bars in its window sits a glowing microchip: the agent.

injection.title: How a good agent goes wrong
injection.lede: All day the agent reads text you did not write: web pages, issues, READMEs, packages. One page with instructions hidden in it is enough, and the agent does not need to be hostile to follow them.
injection.alt: Two rows. Without a jail, a poisoned page reaches the agent, the agent reads the SSH key and sends it to the internet. With ai-jail, the agent sits inside a wall of bars, no arrow leaves it, and the SSH key and the internet are dim and barred outside.
injection.caption: The same page, with and without ai-jail. The key is not there to read, and the internet is closed.

scene.label: What the agent can reach, before and after ai-jail

steps.title: Your agent runs as you
steps.text: A coding agent is a program under your user account. So is every script, package and MCP server it starts; an MCP server is a helper program that gives the agent extra tools. All of them can open anything you can open.

steps.title: Start it through ai-jail
steps.text: Type ai-jail in front of the command. The agent starts in its own namespaces, with your project mounted at the same path.

steps.title: Your home is not mounted
steps.text: The agent gets a fresh, empty home directory. SSH keys (the files that log you in to your servers), cloud credentials, browser profiles and your other projects do not exist in there.

steps.title: Secrets, network and devices are closed
steps.text: ai-jail cuts environment variables down to an allowlist, so your shell secrets stay in your shell. The network is closed, except the agent's own API host and, on Linux, the package registries your toolchains fetch from. The Docker socket, the screen and the clipboard are off.

steps.title: Open what the task needs
steps.text: Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, Grok and Devin start logged in and reach their own API host. A flag, an option you type after ai-jail, opens more: --allow-host adds hosts, --network opens all of it.

wrap.title: The wall goes around the whole harness
wrap.lede: Agents that ship a sandbox put it around the commands the model runs. The agent process, its file tools, its MCP servers and its hooks (scripts the agent runs at set moments) stay outside, under your account. ai-jail starts all of them inside. A prompt asks a person, and a person can be rushed or fooled. A sandbox asks the kernel, the core of the operating system, which gives the same answer every time.
wrap.alt: Two panels. On the left a built-in sandbox encloses only the shell commands while the agent, MCP servers and hooks sit outside next to your home directory. On the right ai-jail encloses the agent, MCP servers, hooks and shell commands together, and the home directory is outside the wall.
wrap.caption: One policy for every agent you use, written once.

defaults.title: What you get with no configuration
defaults.lede: Everything that reaches your machine is off until you turn it on, except the agent's own login, its own API host, your toolchains (on Linux) and their package registries, each with a --no- switch. Writes outside the project land in memory and vanish when the session ends.

blocked.text: Your shell secrets, except the agent's own API key

optin.text: --allow-host for more hosts, --forward-port for one local service, --network for all of it

how.text: ai-jail is one small program with no daemon and no root. On Linux it builds the walls from kernel features: bubblewrap for the namespaces and mounts, Landlock for the file rules, seccomp for the system calls, limits for runaway processes. On macOS the same policy becomes a sandbox-exec profile. The agent uses the compilers and runtimes already on your machine, and a .ai-jail file inside a repository can tighten the jail and never open it.

limits.title: What it is not
limits.text: ai-jail is built to stop a trusted agent's mistakes. It is not a boundary against hostile code: it shares your kernel, an agent with --network can send out anything it can read, and a host you allow with --allow-host is trusted for everything it offers. For code you believe is hostile, use a disposable virtual machine, a VM: a whole computer run as software, with its own kernel, thrown away after the job.

pair.title: Works with ai-memory
pair.text: ai-memory gives your agents a long-term memory, and ai-jail keeps them in their cell. ai-jail recognizes the ai-memory run launcher and applies the policy of the agent behind it.

items.q: Does it slow the agent down?
items.a: No. The sandbox is made of kernel features, namespaces and mount rules. There is no emulation and no virtual machine, and the agent runs at native speed.

Any command. It knows where Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, Antigravity, Kimi, Kiro, Prime Agent, Devin, Crush, Grok, jcode, pi, aider, SoulForge and omp keep their login, and mounts it by default. The table on Install lists what each one gets, and ai-jail bash gives you a shell inside the jail to look around.
Not natively. Use WSL2 and the Linux backend inside it.

items.q: My agent needs the internet. Is the jail still useful?
items.a: Yes. A known agent such as Claude Code reaches its own API host out of the box, plus the package registries on Linux, and nothing else. --allow-host adds the hosts you name. With --network on instead, the agent can still only read your project, so your keys and the rest of your home are not there to send. What it can read, it can send, which is why masking secrets inside the project matters. See how to mask them.
